q: A wagon placed for unloading at a goods shed is not released by the consignee long after the free time allowed for unloading has expired, and the station levies a charge for the detention of the wagon beyond that free time. The charge so levied is called:
e: Demurrage is the charge levied for detention of a wagon beyond the free time allowed for loading or unloading.

q: Goods unloaded at a station are not removed by the consignee within the free time allowed for their removal, and the station levies a charge for the ground occupied by the goods at the station beyond that free time. The charge so levied is called:
e: Wharfage is the charge levied for ground occupied by goods at a station beyond the free time allowed for their removal, distinct from demurrage on wagons.

q: A through consignment travels over three zonal railways under a single Railway Receipt, and the total freight collected on it has to be divided among the three railways. This division of the earnings of through traffic among the railways over which the traffic has passed is known as:
e: Division of through traffic earnings among the railways over which the traffic passed is called apportionment of earnings.

q: A zonal railway reports, for a review, the earnings of the traffic which began its journey on its own lines, before any division of through earnings with other railways is made. The earnings so reported are its:
e: Earnings of traffic originating on a railway's own lines, before division of through earnings with other railways, are its originating earnings.

q: At the close of a ten-day period, a station has collected its earnings in cash and deposited them with the bank, but the amount has not yet been credited in the accounts of the railway by the close of that period. In the earnings accounts, such an amount is broadly described as:
e: Station earnings collected and deposited with the bank but not yet credited in railway accounts by the close of the period are cash in transit.

q: At a location away from the railway station premises, an authorised agent sells unreserved tickets to passengers on behalf of the Railways under a scheme meant to take unreserved ticketing closer to the public. Such an agent is known as a:
e: A Jansadharan Ticket Booking Sevak is an authorised agent away from station premises who sells unreserved tickets to take unreserved ticketing closer to the public.

q: An operating officer wants to follow, on the Freight Operations Information System, the movement and current position of rakes and wagons carrying goods traffic across the network. The module of the system which principally deals with rake and wagon movement and management is the:
e: In FOIS, the Rake Management System module principally deals with rake and wagon movement, placement and management for goods traffic.

q: A passenger at a station buys an unreserved ticket for an ordinary passenger train from a counter working on the system installed by the Railways for issuing unreserved tickets through computerised counters. This system is the:
e: Unreserved tickets through computerised counters are issued under the Unreserved Ticketing System (UTS), distinct from the Passenger Reservation System for reserved tickets.

q: At the close of the day, a booking clerk returns to the stock a number of printed tickets which were never issued to any passenger, and these tickets are sent on for check. In the Traffic Accounts Office, such tickets are dealt with as:
e: Printed tickets returned to stock without ever being issued are non-issued tickets, accounted for separately from collected tickets.

q: Tickets collected from passengers at the destination and during travel are received in the Traffic Accounts Office for check. The check of collected tickets is exercised mainly to ensure that:

options.A: The tickets were printed at the authorised press
options.B: Every ticket issued and collected is duly accounted for and no collected ticket is used again
options.C: The passengers travelled only up to the stations printed on the tickets
options.D: The fare printed on the ticket is the highest fare for the class

e: Check of collected tickets ensures every ticket issued and collected is duly accounted for and no collected ticket is reused or escapes accountal.

q: An operating officer explains to a trainee that a wagon which is loaded today begins a fresh cycle of use when it is loaded again after being unloaded and moved for its next load. The average time taken by a wagon to complete one such cycle, from one loading to the next, is the:
e: Wagon turn-round is the average time for a wagon to complete one cycle from one loading to the next loading, after unloading and movement for the next load.

q: A costing trainee is told that the Gross Tonne Kilometres performed by goods trains on a railway are always more than the Net Tonne Kilometres performed on it. This is because Gross Tonne Kilometres include, in addition to the weight of the paying load:

options.A: The weight of the passengers carried in the trains
options.B: The tare (empty) weight of the wagons carrying the load
options.C: The weight of the station buildings on the section
options.D: The weight of the fuel consumed during the run

e: Gross Tonne Kilometres exceed Net Tonne Kilometres because they include, besides the paying load, the tare or empty weight of the wagons carrying it.

q: A commercial officer wants, for a commodity-wise review, the tonnes originated and the earnings of each principal commodity carried by his railway during a month. The monthly statement which principally gives this commodity-wise information is:
e: Statement 7C gives commodity-wise details of tonnes originated and earnings for principal commodities carried during the month.

q: The Railway Board requires a quick figure of the gross earnings of the Railways for the first ten days of a month, long before the accounts of the month are closed. The figure supplied for this purpose is the:

options.A: Final audited earnings of the month
options.B: Ten-day statement of approximate gross earnings
options.C: Appropriation Account figure for the period
options.D: Apportioned earnings statement of the month

e: The ten-day statement of approximate gross earnings gives a quick figure of gross earnings for the first ten days long before monthly accounts are closed.

q: A passenger pays, over and above the ordinary fare for his class, an additional charge for the facility of booking his reserved ticket at short notice under the special scheme for last-minute reservations. This additional charge is the:
e: The additional charge for last-minute reservation under the special scheme over and above the ordinary fare is the Tatkal charge.

q: A daily commuter buys a ticket which entitles him to travel any number of times, during the period of its validity, between the two stations named on it. The ticket bought by him is a:
e: A season ticket entitles the holder to unlimited travel between the two named stations during its period of validity.

q: Before a wagon placed for loading can be detained without charge, the Railways allow the consignor a prescribed period within which the loading is to be completed free of detention charges. This period allowed free of charge is known as:
e: Free time is the prescribed period allowed for loading or unloading a wagon without detention or demurrage charges.

q: A consignor elects to book his goods at the lower rate available when the Railways are not liable for the risks of carriage in the ordinary way, and the Railway Receipt is endorsed accordingly. The consignment so booked is said to be booked at:
e: Booking at owner's risk means the consignor accepts the lower rate with the Railways not liable for carriage risks in the ordinary way, and the Railway Receipt is endorsed accordingly.

q: Before his goods are accepted for booking, a consignor executes and hands in at the forwarding station a document declaring the particulars of the consignment and the conditions on which it is offered for carriage. This document is the:
e: The Forwarding Note is executed by the consignor before booking, declaring particulars of the consignment and the conditions on which it is offered for carriage.

q: The owner of a private siding adjoining a station is charged, in addition to the freight on his traffic, for the services rendered by the Railways in placing and removing wagons at his siding. The charge so levied for the use of, and services at, the siding is a:
e: Siding charges are levied on a private siding owner, in addition to freight, for placing and removing wagons and other services rendered at the siding.

q: A finance trainee is corrected when he treats the words 'earnings' and 'revenue' of the Railways as meaning exactly the same thing. The correct distinction is that traffic earnings represent:

options.A: Only the cash actually received at stations during the period
options.B: Only the refunds and remissions allowed during the period
options.C: The total budgetary receipts of the Government of India
options.D: The amounts earned from traffic operations during the period, whether realised in cash or yet to be realised

e: Traffic earnings are amounts earned from traffic operations during the period whether realised in cash or yet to be realised, on an accrual basis, unlike cash receipts alone.

q: At the close of a period, the Traffic Suspense account of a railway shows a credit balance, representing amounts collected by its stations on traffic account which are still to be adjusted against the proper earnings and other heads. A credit balance under Traffic Suspense broadly indicates:

options.A: Traffic dues yet to be recovered from the public
options.B: Amounts realised on traffic account and awaiting adjustment to the proper heads
options.C: Loss suffered on goods traffic during the period
options.D: Working expenses yet to be paid by the railway

e: A credit balance under Traffic Suspense indicates amounts realised by stations on traffic account still awaiting adjustment to proper earnings and other heads.

q: A merchant books a consignment at one station for a destination on a distant railway, paying the full freight at the time of booking itself. In goods traffic, booking under which the freight is paid at the forwarding station at the time of booking is known as:
e: Paid booking means freight is paid in full at the forwarding station at the time of booking, as against to-pay booking where it is collected at destination.

q: A passenger leaves his luggage for safe custody at a station facility on payment of the prescribed charges and takes it back on his return after producing the receipt given to him. The facility at the station where luggage is so kept in safe custody is the:
e: The cloak room is the station facility where luggage is kept in safe custody on payment of prescribed charges against a receipt, and returned on its production.

q: A consignment booked at a station on one railway is carried through to its destination on another railway, without any fresh booking on the way, under the original Railway Receipt. Such traffic, which passes over more than one railway under a single booking, is known as:
e: Through traffic passes over more than one railway under a single booking and original Railway Receipt, without fresh booking en route.

q: A station accountant is closing the monthly Station Balance Sheet. The opening outstanding balance of the month was Rs 5,50,000, the earnings and other debits of the month were Rs 16,80,000, and the remittances and other credits of the month were Rs 19,10,000. The closing outstanding balance of the station works out to:
e: Closing outstanding equals opening outstanding plus debits minus credits. Here Rs 5,50,000 + Rs 16,80,000 - Rs 19,10,000 = Rs 3,20,000.

q: The statistical cell of a zonal railway has to report the total track kilometres of a section whose route length is 95 kilometres, laid with two running lines throughout, and which has, in addition, 36 kilometres of sidings, yard lines and crossings. The total track kilometres of the section work out to:
e: Track kilometres count each running line separately. Here 95 x 2 = 190 km of running lines, plus 36 km of sidings and yard lines = 226 km.

q: A costing officer is verifying a loco shed's monthly return, which shows that the goods locomotives consumed 6,000 litres of diesel oil during the month while performing 20,00,000 Gross Tonne Kilometres. On verification, the Specific Fuel Consumption of the locomotives works out to:
e: Specific Fuel Consumption equals fuel consumed divided by Gross Tonne Kilometres, per 1000 GTKM. Here 6,000 / 20,00,000 x 1000 = 3.0 litres per 1000 GTKM.

q: During a month, the locomotives in electric traction on a railway consumed 80,000 kWh of electrical energy and performed 40,00,000 Gross Tonne Kilometres. The Specific Energy Consumption of the railway for the month works out to:
e: Specific Energy Consumption equals energy consumed divided by Gross Tonne Kilometres, per 1000 GTKM. Here 80,000 / 40,00,000 x 1000 = 20 kWh per 1000 GTKM.

q: At an occupancy review, a division reports that against 80,00,000 seat kilometres offered during the period, its coaching services actually performed 60,00,000 passenger kilometres. The load factor (occupation ratio) reported for the coaching services works out to:
e: Load factor equals passenger kilometres divided by seat kilometres offered, as a percentage. Here 60,00,000 / 80,00,000 x 100 = 75 per cent.

q: A finance officer is reviewing the annual results of a zonal railway whose gross earnings for the year are Rs 6,000 crore and whose working expenses are Rs 5,700 crore. The Operating Ratio of the railway for the year works out to:
e: Operating Ratio equals working expenses divided by gross earnings, as a percentage. Here Rs 5,700 crore / Rs 6,000 crore x 100 = 95 per cent.

q: A statistics clerk is closing the monthly wagon performance return of a railway. During the month, the total wagon days on the railway were 15,00,000 and the number of wagons loaded was 3,00,000. The wagon turn-round for the month works out to:
e: Wagon turn-round equals total wagon days divided by number of wagons loaded. Here 15,00,000 / 3,00,000 = 5.0 days.

q: A costing officer has to work out the average lead of the goods traffic of a railway which performed 2,70,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres during a period in which the tonnes carried were 3,00,000. The average lead of goods traffic of the railway works out to:
e: Average lead of goods traffic equals Net Tonne Kilometres divided by tonnes carried. Here 2,70,00,000 / 3,00,000 = 90 kilometres.

q: A performance analyst has to work out the Net Tonne Kilometres per engine day of a railway which performed 84,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres during a period in which the goods engine days numbered 1,400. The Net Tonne Kilometres per engine day work out to:
e: Net Tonne Kilometres per engine day equal Net Tonne Kilometres divided by goods engine days. Here 84,00,000 / 1,400 = 6,000.

q: A performance analyst has to work out the Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day of a railway which performed 33,60,000 Net Tonne Kilometres during a period in which the wagon days numbered 80,000. The Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day work out to:
e: Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day equal Net Tonne Kilometres divided by wagon days. Here 33,60,000 / 80,000 = 42.

q: A traffic costing cell has worked out that the total cost of the goods services of a railway for a period is Rs 72,00,000 and the Net Tonne Kilometres performed are 16,00,000. The cost per Net Tonne Kilometre works out to:
e: Cost per Net Tonne Kilometre equals total cost of goods services divided by Net Tonne Kilometres. Here Rs 72,00,000 / 16,00,000 = Rs 4.50.

q: A traffic costing cell has worked out that the total cost of the coaching services of a railway for a period is Rs 1,08,00,000 and the passenger kilometres performed are 2,70,00,000. The cost per passenger kilometre works out to:
e: Cost per passenger kilometre equals total cost of coaching services divided by passenger kilometres. Here Rs 1,08,00,000 / 2,70,00,000 = Rs 0.40.

q: During a period, the total wagon kilometres run on a railway were 85,00,000, of which the empty wagon kilometres were 17,00,000. The percentage of empty wagon kilometres to total wagon kilometres is:
e: Percentage of empty wagon kilometres equals empty wagon kilometres divided by total wagon kilometres, as a percentage. Here 17,00,000 / 85,00,000 x 100 = 20 per cent.

q: The passenger earnings of a railway for a period are Rs 2,10,00,000 and the number of passengers carried during the period is 30,00,000. The earnings per passenger of the railway for the period are:
e: Earnings per passenger equal passenger earnings divided by passengers carried. Here Rs 2,10,00,000 / 30,00,000 = Rs 7.

q: The gross earnings of a railway for a period are Rs 8,40,00,000. During the same period it performed 60,00,000 passenger kilometres and 1,50,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres. The earnings per traffic unit of the railway work out to:
e: Earnings per traffic unit equal gross earnings divided by total traffic units. Here Rs 8,40,00,000 / (60,00,000 + 1,50,00,000) = Rs 8,40,00,000 / 2,10,00,000 = Rs 4.00.

q: A railway performed 1,04,00,000 passenger kilometres during a period in which the passenger train kilometres run were 16,000. The average number of passengers carried per train on the railway works out to:
e: Average passengers per train equal passenger kilometres divided by passenger train kilometres. Here 1,04,00,000 / 16,000 = 650.

q: The Net Tonne Kilometres performed on a railway are 7,20,00,000 and the loaded wagon kilometres are 18,00,000. The average load of a loaded wagon on the railway works out to:
e: Average load of a loaded wagon equals Net Tonne Kilometres divided by loaded wagon kilometres. Here 7,20,00,000 / 18,00,000 = 40 tonnes.

q: A loco foreman is checking a monthly return which shows that the locomotives of a railway ran 16,80,000 engine kilometres during the month and the engine days numbered 4,000. The engine kilometres per engine day work out to:
e: Engine kilometres per engine day equal engine kilometres divided by engine days. Here 16,80,000 / 4,000 = 420.

q: A statistics clerk has to report the density of passenger traffic on a railway which performed 2,52,00,000 passenger kilometres during a year in which the route kilometres open for traffic were 6,000. The density of passenger traffic on the railway works out to:
e: Density of passenger traffic equals passenger kilometres divided by route kilometres open. Here 2,52,00,000 / 6,000 = 4,200 passenger kilometres per route kilometre.

q: The goods earnings of a railway for a period are Rs 1,62,00,000 and the goods train kilometres run during the period are 1,80,000. The earnings per goods train kilometre work out to:
e: Earnings per goods train kilometre equal goods earnings divided by goods train kilometres. Here Rs 1,62,00,000 / 1,80,000 = Rs 90.

q: A costing officer has to work out the average lead of passenger traffic of a railway which performed 1,80,00,000 passenger kilometres during a period in which the passengers carried numbered 30,00,000. The average lead of passenger traffic works out to:
e: Average lead of passenger traffic equals passenger kilometres divided by passengers carried. Here 1,80,00,000 / 30,00,000 = 60 kilometres.

q: A train covers a distance of 300 kilometres in a total time of 6 hours, of which 1 hour is spent in halts at intermediate stations. The running speed of the train, which excludes the time spent in halts, works out to:
e: Running speed excludes halt time, so it equals distance divided by running time only. Here running time is 6 - 1 = 5 hours, and 300 / 5 = 60 kilometres per hour.

q: The earnings of a railway for a period consist of coaching earnings of Rs 2,40,00,000, goods earnings of Rs 5,60,00,000 and sundry other earnings of Rs 20,00,000. The gross traffic earnings of the railway for the period work out to:
e: Gross traffic earnings equal coaching plus goods plus sundry earnings. Here Rs 2,40,00,000 + Rs 5,60,00,000 + Rs 20,00,000 = Rs 8,20,00,000.

q: A passenger train offering 1,200 seats runs over a distance of 400 kilometres. The seat kilometres offered by the train on the run work out to:
e: Seat kilometres offered equal seats multiplied by distance run. Here 1,200 x 400 = 4,80,000 seat kilometres.

q: A goods clerk has to report the tonnes carried by his railway during a period. The tonnes originated (loaded) on the railway were 2,00,000 and the tonnes received from other railways were 50,000. The tonnes carried by the railway during the period work out to:
e: Tonnes carried equal tonnes originated plus tonnes received from other railways. Here 2,00,000 + 50,000 = 2,50,000 tonnes.

q: A coaching statistics clerk has to work out the vehicle kilometres performed by a train of 14 vehicles which runs 6,000 train kilometres during a period. The vehicle kilometres performed work out to:
e: Vehicle kilometres equal number of vehicles in the train multiplied by train kilometres run. Here 14 x 6,000 = 84,000.

q: A goods statistics clerk has to work out the available tonne kilometres offered by a railway whose wagons, of an average carrying capacity of 60 tonnes, ran 1,60,000 wagon kilometres during a period. The available tonne kilometres offered work out to:
e: Available tonne kilometres equal average carrying capacity multiplied by wagon kilometres run. Here 60 x 1,60,000 = 96,00,000.

q: A statistics clerk is reporting the extent of a section which has three running lines laid over a route length of 50 kilometres. For the purpose of reporting the route kilometres of the section, the correct figure is:

options.A: 150 route kilometres, counting each running line separately
options.B: 100 route kilometres, counting two of the running lines
options.C: 50 route kilometres, the section being counted once irrespective of the number of lines
options.D: 200 route kilometres, adding an allowance for the sidings

e: Route kilometres count a section once irrespective of the number of running lines laid over it, so a 50 km section remains 50 route kilometres.

q: A section has a route length of 80 kilometres with two running lines throughout, besides 30 kilometres of sidings and yard lines. The running track kilometres of the section, which cover the running lines only, work out to:
e: Running track kilometres cover running lines only, excluding sidings. Here 80 x 2 = 160 kilometres for the two running lines.

q: A commercial clerk is compiling the traffic figures of his railway and has to state what the tonnes originated on the railway represent. The tonnes originated on a railway represent the tonnes of goods traffic which are:

options.A: Loaded at the stations of that railway
options.B: Received from other railways at interchange points
options.C: Unloaded at the stations of that railway
options.D: Carried over that railway on through bookings only

e: Tonnes originated are the tonnes of goods traffic loaded at stations of that railway itself, distinct from tonnes received from other railways.

q: A commuter travelling daily between two suburban stations asks the booking clerk about the short-distance electric trains in which he travels. The EMU trains used on such suburban services are:

options.A: Diesel multiple unit trains worked by a separate locomotive
options.B: Electric Multiple Unit trains, with traction distributed over the coaches of the train set
options.C: Steam-hauled trains reserved for suburban traffic
options.D: Goods trains adapted for carrying passengers

e: EMU trains are Electric Multiple Unit trains with traction distributed over the coaches of the set, used mainly for suburban services.

q: A consignor elects to book his consignment at the owner's risk rate, at which the Railways do not accept liability for the risks of carriage in the ordinary way. Before the consignment is accepted at that rate, the consignor is required to execute a:

options.A: Forwarding Note only, with no other document
options.B: Indemnity bond in favour of the consignee
options.C: Risk Note, undertaking the risk on the prescribed conditions
options.D: Bank guarantee for the value of the goods

e: Before acceptance at owner's risk rate, the consignor must execute a Risk Note undertaking the risk on the prescribed conditions.

q: A passenger holds a confirmed reserved ticket for a train which the Railways cancel altogether and do not run. In regard to the refund due to the passenger, the correct position is that he is entitled to:

options.A: Refund of the fare after deduction of the cancellation charges
options.B: Refund of the fare after deduction of the reservation charge only
options.C: No refund, as the cancellation was beyond his control
options.D: Full refund of the fare paid, without any deduction

e: Where the Railways cancel a train altogether and do not run it, the passenger gets a full refund of the fare paid without any deduction.

q: A passenger's e-ticket remains fully waitlisted even after the preparation of the reservation chart of the train. In regard to such a waitlisted e-ticket, the correct position is that:

options.A: The passenger can travel in the reserved coach on payment of the excess charge
options.B: The ticket is automatically cancelled and the fare is refunded to the account through which it was booked
options.C: The passenger must file a Ticket Deposit Receipt at the destination station for the refund
options.D: The ticket is converted into an unreserved ticket for the same train

e: A fully waitlisted e-ticket remaining waitlisted after chart preparation is automatically cancelled and the fare is refunded to the account used for booking.

q: A private party takes on lease the parcel space in the brake vans (SLRs) of specified trains and carries parcel traffic in that space on payment of the lease charges to the Railways. The earnings so realised by the Railways from the leasing of parcel space are classified under:

options.D: Miscellaneous receipts of the Commercial Department

e: Parcel traffic, including earnings from leasing of SLR parcel space, is classified under coaching earnings as other coaching earnings.

q: At the close of a month, the balance shown by the Accounts Office Balance Sheet of a zonal railway does not agree with the balance under Traffic Suspense in the general books of the railway. The correct inference from this disagreement is that:

options.A: The difference indicates an error or an unadjusted item which has to be traced and reconciled
options.B: The Accounts Office Balance Sheet is to be altered to match the general books without enquiry
options.C: The Traffic Suspense head is to be closed for the month
options.D: The stations are to be debited with the amount of the difference at once

e: Disagreement between the Accounts Office Balance Sheet and Traffic Suspense in the general books indicates an error or unadjusted item to be traced and reconciled, not adjusted without enquiry.

q: A station on a zonal railway does not remit its daily earnings through the traffic Cash Office, but deposits them with a designated branch of the accredited bank under the arrangement in force for such deposits. The branch so designated for receiving the earnings of stations is known as a:
e: The designated bank branch receiving station earnings under the bank deposit arrangement in lieu of the traffic Cash Office is the focal point branch.

q: A passenger pays, over and above the ordinary fare, the Tatkal premium for booking a reserved ticket at short notice, and asks how the amount is treated in the earnings of the Railways. The Tatkal premium so collected forms part of:
e: The Tatkal premium collected over the ordinary fare forms part of coaching or passenger earnings of the Railways.

q: A tourist group travels on a theme-based tourist circuit train which is run, under the policy of the Railways, by a service provider using railway infrastructure and coaches. Such theme-based tourist circuit trains are run under the:
e: Theme-based tourist circuit trains run by service providers on railway infrastructure and coaches are operated under the Bharat Gaurav trains policy.

q: A private developer proposes to set up a cargo terminal entirely on his own land away from any station, connected to the serving station by a rail link, and to handle rail traffic there. Under the Gati Shakti Multi-Modal Cargo Terminal policy, such a terminal:

options.A: Can be developed only on railway land
options.B: Cannot be developed at all for rail traffic
options.C: Can be developed on non-railway (private) land as well, by the terminal developer
options.D: Can be developed only inside a Private Freight Terminal

e: Under the Gati Shakti Multi-Modal Cargo Terminal policy, a cargo terminal can be developed on non-railway private land as well by the terminal developer, connected by a rail link.

q: A consignment carried by rail is destroyed by an unprecedented flood, an act of God, while in transit, without any negligence on the part of the Railways. In regard to the liability of the railway administration for the loss, the correct position is that the Railways are:

options.A: Liable as insurer of the goods against all risks
options.B: Liable to pay the full market value of the goods in every case
options.C: Liable only if the consignor had paid the percentage charge
options.D: Not liable for loss caused by an act of God, which is one of the excepted causes of loss

e: Loss caused by an act of God without railway negligence is an excepted cause, and the Railways are not liable for such loss in transit.

q: A licensee runs pay-and-use toilets at a station under a contract with the Railways and pays the licence fee due under the contract to the station. The licence fee so received is classified in the earnings of the Railways under:
e: Licence fees from pay-and-use toilets and similar commercial licences at stations are classified under sundry other earnings.

q: A passenger who has arrived at a station for an onward journey the next morning wishes to book a retiring room at the station for the night without visiting the station office. Retiring rooms and dormitories at stations can be booked online through the portal of the:

options.C: Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation

e: Retiring rooms and dormitories at stations can be booked online through the portal of the Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation (IRCTC).

q: Postal mail bags are carried by a passenger train under the arrangement between the Railways and the postal authorities, and the charges for the carriage are accounted for by the Railways. These charges for the carriage of mails are classified under:
e: Charges for carriage of postal mails by passenger trains are classified under coaching earnings.

q: A licensed private container train operator runs container trains over the railway network and pays haulage charges to the Railways for the use of the network. The haulage charges so received by the Railways are classified under:
e: Haulage charges received from private container train operators for use of the railway network are classified under goods earnings.

q: The coaching earnings of a railway for a period are Rs 1,10,00,000 and the coaching train kilometres run during the period are 1,00,000. The earnings per coaching train kilometre of the railway work out to:
e: Earnings per coaching train kilometre equal coaching earnings divided by coaching train kilometres. Here Rs 1,10,00,000 / 1,00,000 = Rs 110.

q: A wagon performance analyst has to work out the wagon kilometres per wagon day of a railway whose wagons ran 18,00,000 wagon kilometres during a period in which the wagon days numbered 15,000. The wagon kilometres per wagon day work out to:
e: Wagon kilometres per wagon day equal wagon kilometres divided by wagon days. Here 18,00,000 / 15,000 = 120.

q: An operating officer has to work out the Gross Tonne Kilometres per engine day of a railway which performed 72,00,000 Gross Tonne Kilometres during a period in which the engine days numbered 2,400. The Gross Tonne Kilometres per engine day work out to:
e: Gross Tonne Kilometres per engine day equal Gross Tonne Kilometres divided by engine days. Here 72,00,000 / 2,400 = 3,000.

q: The Gross Tonne Kilometres performed on a railway during a period are 2,10,00,000 and the goods train kilometres run are 60,000. The average gross load of goods trains on the railway works out to:
e: Average gross load of goods trains equals Gross Tonne Kilometres divided by goods train kilometres. Here 2,10,00,000 / 60,000 = 350 tonnes.

q: A costing officer is verifying a loco shed's monthly return, which shows that the goods locomotives consumed 10,500 litres of diesel oil during the month while performing 25,00,000 Gross Tonne Kilometres. The Specific Fuel Consumption of the locomotives works out to:
e: Specific Fuel Consumption equals fuel consumed divided by Gross Tonne Kilometres, per 1000 GTKM. Here 10,500 / 25,00,000 x 1000 = 4.2 litres per 1000 GTKM.

q: A statistics clerk has to report the density of goods traffic on a railway which performed 4,80,00,000 Gross Tonne Kilometres during a year in which the route kilometres open for traffic were 3,000. The density of goods traffic on the railway works out to:

options.A: 1,600 Gross Tonne Kilometres per route kilometre
options.B: 1,60,000 Gross Tonne Kilometres per route kilometre
options.C: 16,000 Gross Tonne Kilometres per route kilometre
options.D: 160 Gross Tonne Kilometres per route kilometre

e: Density of goods traffic equals Gross Tonne Kilometres divided by route kilometres open. Here 4,80,00,000 / 3,000 = 16,000 Gross Tonne Kilometres per route kilometre.

q: A coaching statistics clerk has to report the total passengers carried by his railway during a period. The passengers who began their journey on the railway were 4,50,000 and the passengers received from other railways were 1,50,000. The passengers carried by the railway during the period work out to:
e: Passengers carried equal passengers originating on the railway plus passengers received from other railways. Here 4,50,000 + 1,50,000 = 6,00,000.

q: A performance analyst has to work out the average speed of the goods trains of a railway which ran 24,000 goods train kilometres during a period in which the goods trains took 800 train hours in all. The average speed of the goods trains works out to:
e: Average speed of goods trains equals goods train kilometres divided by train hours. Here 24,000 / 800 = 30 kilometres per hour.

q: A goods statistics clerk has to work out the average number of wagons per goods train on a railway which ran 12,00,000 goods wagon kilometres during a period in which the goods train kilometres run were 25,000. The average number of wagons per goods train works out to:
e: Average wagons per goods train equal goods wagon kilometres divided by goods train kilometres. Here 12,00,000 / 25,000 = 48.

q: A traffic costing cell has to work out the average rate realised per tonne kilometre on the goods traffic of a railway whose goods earnings for a period are Rs 1,12,00,000 and which performed 32,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres during the period. The average rate realised per tonne kilometre works out to:
e: Average rate per tonne kilometre equals goods earnings divided by Net Tonne Kilometres. Here Rs 1,12,00,000 / 32,00,000 = Rs 3.50.

q: A statistics clerk is preparing the monthly return giving the details of the through, van and shunting goods trains run on his railway, for submission with the other statistical statements. The monthly statistical statement which gives these details is:
e: Statement 3-B is the monthly statistical statement giving details of through, van and shunting goods trains run.

q: A loco shed officer has to render the monthly return of the fuel consumed and the power generated and consumed on his railway, covering coal, diesel oil and electrical energy. The monthly statistical statement which deals with fuel and power statistics is:
e: Statement 5-A is the monthly statistical statement dealing with fuel and power statistics, covering coal, diesel oil and electrical energy.

q: A reservation supervisor is asked by a trainee to name the computer software on which the Passenger Reservation System of Indian Railways operates at the reservation centres. The software is known as:
e: The Passenger Reservation System at reservation centres operates on the CONCERT software.

q: A newly posted accounts officer asks who has developed, and who maintains, the large information systems of Indian Railways such as the Passenger Reservation System and the Freight Operations Information System. These systems have been developed and are maintained by the:
e: The large information systems of Indian Railways such as PRS and FOIS have been developed and are maintained by the Centre for Railway Information Systems (CRIS).

q: A commercial officer is asked to suggest a novel idea, outside the usual fare and freight earnings, for earning additional income for the Railways from an unused asset at his station, and to forward it under the scheme meant for generating non-fare revenue through new and innovative ideas. That scheme is:
e: NINFRIS, the New Innovative Non Fare Revenue Ideas Scheme, invites novel ideas outside fare and freight to earn non-fare revenue from unused assets.

q: A passenger's booking status for a journey beginning at an important intermediate station of a train's route, where a separate quota of accommodation is allotted for that station, is shown as RLWL. In the Passenger Reservation System, RLWL stands for:
e: In PRS, RLWL stands for Remote Location Waiting List, applicable to journeys beginning at an important intermediate station with a separate quota.

q: A traveller books his reserved ticket, not at a station reservation office, but at the counter of a licensed agent in the city who is authorised by the Railways to issue reserved and unreserved tickets from his own premises. Such an authorised agent is a:
e: A Yatri Ticket Suvidha Kendra licensee is a licensed city agent authorised to issue reserved and unreserved tickets from his own premises.

q: A station receives its Advice of Internal Check showing a debit for a deficiency in its accounts, but the error sheet detailing the error has not yet reached the station. The station master proposes to wait for the error sheet before taking the debit to account. The correct position is that the debit advised through the Advice of Internal Check is to be taken to account by the station:

options.A: Only after the error sheet is received and verified
options.B: Only after the close of the financial year
options.C: Whether or not the error sheet has been received
options.D: Only with the prior sanction of the Divisional Commercial Manager

e: A debit advised through the Advice of Internal Check must be taken to account by the station whether or not the detailed error sheet has been received.

q: At the close of a day, a station is found to have remitted to the bank an amount smaller than the earnings it had collected during the day. In regard to the deficiency so found, the correct treatment is that it is:

options.A: Debited to the station and shown as outstanding against it
options.B: Written off at the station itself as a cash shortage
options.C: Adjusted against the earnings of the following month without any debit
options.D: Borne by the traffic Cash Office

e: A deficiency where remittance to the bank is less than earnings collected is debited to the station and shown as outstanding against it until cleared.

q: A station has exhausted its stock of printed card tickets and needs a fresh supply for sale to passengers. In regard to the supply and accountal of such ticket stock, the correct position is that printed card tickets and blank paper tickets are supplied to stations:

options.A: By direct purchase by the station master from the local market
options.B: Only once at the time the station is opened for traffic
options.C: By the Railway Press without any record of the quantities supplied
options.D: Against indents, and the accountal of the ticket stock is watched in the Traffic Accounts Office

e: Printed card tickets and blank paper tickets are supplied to stations against indents, and accountal of ticket stock is watched in the Traffic Accounts Office.

q: A catering contractor at a station has fallen behind in paying the licence fee due under his contract, and the matter comes up in the Traffic Accounts Office. In respect of such catering and other commercial contracts at stations, one of the functions of the Traffic Accounts Office is to ensure that:

options.A: The menus and prices of the catering unit are fixed by the Accounts Office
options.B: The licence fees and other dues recoverable under the contracts are fully recovered
options.C: The staff of the contractor are paid by the Railways
options.D: The contract is renewed automatically on its expiry

e: For catering and other commercial contracts, Traffic Accounts ensures licence fees and other dues recoverable under the contracts are fully recovered.

q: An accounts clerk is listing the items that make up the accounts rendered by a goods shed of a station. Which of the following does NOT form part of the accounts rendered by the goods shed?

options.A: Freight collected on goods traffic booked and delivered
options.B: Demurrage and wharfage charges accrued at the shed
options.C: Pay and allowances of the goods shed staff
options.D: Siding charges recoverable from siding owners

e: Goods shed accounts cover freight, demurrage, wharfage and siding charges, but pay and allowances of goods shed staff are establishment accounts, not goods shed traffic accounts.

q: A statistics trainee asks how the passenger kilometres performed on a railway during a month are arrived at from the returns of the stations. Passenger kilometres are computed as:

options.A: The seating capacity of the trains multiplied by the train kilometres run
options.B: The number of passengers booked multiplied by the route length of the railway
options.C: The earnings of the railway divided by the average fare per passenger
options.D: The sum, over all passengers, of the distance travelled by each passenger

e: Passenger kilometres are the sum, over all passengers, of the distance travelled by each passenger, computed from station returns.

q: A zonal railway runs extensive suburban services with electric multiple unit trains in a metropolitan city, and its accounts officer has to classify the earnings of those services. The earnings from suburban (local/EMU) passenger services form part of the:

options.D: Miscellaneous receipts of the operating department

e: Earnings from suburban local and EMU passenger services form part of coaching earnings, like other passenger services.

q: At the end of a month, the headquarters of a zonal railway prepares a report reviewing how the earnings of the month have fared against what was expected of the month. The monthly evaluation report of traffic earnings is used primarily for:

options.A: Fixing the fares and freight rates for the following month
options.B: Comparing the actual earnings with the budget proportions and targets
options.C: Apportioning the earnings of the month among the divisions
options.D: Preparing the salary bills of the commercial staff

e: The monthly evaluation report of traffic earnings is used primarily for comparing actual earnings with budget proportions and targets for the month.

q: A finance officer is preparing the figures to be placed before the Railway Board for the coming financial year in respect of the traffic receipts of his railway. The earnings budget of a railway is:

options.A: The actual earnings realised by the railway during the previous year
options.B: The earnings finally brought to account after internal check
options.C: An estimate of the earnings expected to be realised during the budget year, framed on the basis of the traffic anticipated
options.D: The balance standing under Traffic Suspense at the close of the year

e: The earnings budget is an estimate of earnings expected during the budget year, framed on the basis of traffic anticipated, not past actuals or suspense balances.

q: A merchant asks the goods clerk on what basis the freight payable on his consignment has been fixed, before the distance for its carriage is applied. Freight charges on goods traffic are determined mainly on the basis of:

options.A: The value of the goods as declared by the consignor alone
options.B: The classification of the commodity and the distance over which it is carried
options.C: The number of packages in the consignment alone
options.D: The day of the week on which the consignment is booked

e: Freight charges on goods traffic are determined mainly on the basis of the classification of the commodity and the distance over which it is carried.

q: A coaching statistics clerk has to show separately, in his return, the passengers who began their journey at the stations of his own railway, as distinct from those received from other railways. Such passengers, who commence their journey from stations on that railway, are known as:
e: Passengers commencing their journey from stations on that railway itself are originating passengers, distinct from those received from other railways.

q: The ticket checking staff realise, from a passenger found travelling without a proper ticket, the fare due for his journey together with the excess charge leviable under the Railways Act. The fare and excess charge so realised are accounted for as part of the:

options.C: Miscellaneous receipts of the Commercial Department

e: Fare and excess charge realised by ticket checking staff from passengers without proper tickets are accounted for as part of coaching earnings.

q: Automatic Ticket Vending Machines have been installed at a station and tickets are being sold through them to passengers. In regard to the accountal of the tickets so sold, the correct position is that they are accounted for:

options.A: In the accounts of the station at which the machines are installed
options.B: In the accounts of the Traffic Cash Office direct, bypassing the station
options.C: In the personal accounts of the facilitators attending the machines
options.D: Only in the annual statistical returns of the railway

e: Tickets sold through Automatic Ticket Vending Machines are accounted for in the accounts of the station at which the machines are installed.
